problem: Addition: source says only "a certain qualification"; candidate adds "property".
replacement: American society was not yet prepared to adopt it with all its consequences. The intelligence of New England and the wealth of the country south of the Hudson (as I showed in the preceding chapter) long exercised a kind of aristocratic influence, which tended to keep the exercise of social authority in the hands of a few. Public officials were not all elected, and not all citizens were voters. The right to vote was everywhere kept within certain limits and made to depend on a certain qualification, which was extremely low in the North and higher in the South.

problem: Referent shift: source says the institutions exercise their influence over the community; candidate makes it influence over the mores.
replacement: To explain to the reader the general principles on which the political organization of the counties and townships of the United States rests, I have thought it best to choose one of the States of New England as an example, to examine the workings of its constitution, and then to take a general look over the rest of the country. The township and the county are not organized in the same way in every part of the Union. Still, it is easy to see that the same principles guided the formation of both throughout the Union. I am inclined to believe that these principles have been carried further in New England than elsewhere, and that they therefore give a foreigner more opportunity to observe them. The institutions of New England form a complete and orderly whole. Time has sanctioned them, the laws support them, and the mores of the community support them more strongly still, and they exercise an immense influence over that community. They therefore deserve our attention on every count.

problem: Footnote prose left in 1862 wording ("which generally have", "requires the sanction of a law", "peculiar administration"); style note says to modernize a note's own prose.
replacement: b [ The same rules do not apply to the great towns, which generally have a mayor and a corporation divided into two bodies. This, however, is an exception that requires the sanction of a law.—See the Act of February 22, 1822, for appointing the authorities of the city of Boston. It often happens that small towns as well as cities are subject to a special administration. In 1832, 104 townships in the State of New York were governed in this manner.—Williams’ Register.]

problem: Hedge sharpened: "might lead to anarchy" became "would lead to anarchy".
replacement: There are two ways of reducing the force of authority in a nation. The first is to weaken the supreme power at its very root, by forbidding or preventing society from acting in its own defense under certain circumstances. To weaken authority in this way is what is generally called in Europe laying the foundations of freedom. The second way of reducing the influence of authority does not strip society of any of its rights or paralyze its efforts. Instead, it distributes the exercise of its privileges among various hands and multiplies the officials, each of whom is entrusted with the degree of power he needs to do his duty. There may be nations for whom this distribution of social powers might lead to anarchy. But in itself it is not anarchical. The action of authority is indeed made less irresistible and less perilous in this way, but it is not suppressed altogether.
